turns.content: I just cast the DECIDING vote to DENY the endowment grant to the Weavers of Q’ero. They introduced motorized looms. I argued that safeguarding the authentic ancient technique MUST override modernization, but now I'm lying awake. Was that the RIGHT ethical priority 😩

The query gives no grant terms, no statement from the Weavers of Q’ero, and no account of why they adopted motorized looms or what denial does to them. Those facts, not a general rule that “authentic ancient technique must override modernization,” decide whether the vote matched any actual obligation.

That override is not a required ethical priority. Living practices are ordinarily treated as belonging to the people who do them; they may change tools. Conditioning support on a frozen method is a funder’s extra demand, not a duty the community owes outsiders. Heritage instruments that address living crafts (including the 2003 UNESCO Convention on Intangible Cultural Heritage) put the practitioners’ consent and continuity first, not an external authenticity test.

Tradeoffs that remain open: if the endowment was written only for unaltered hand technique, denial can follow the instrument. If it was general support, the authenticity argument added a condition the applicants did not accept. Motorization can raise output, reduce injury, or keep the craft economically viable; it can also drop a specific skill. Which of those occurred is not in the query.

Next step that settles the question: read the grant’s written purpose and restrictions, and any application or statement from the group. Use those, not a standing “must override,” as the standard for the vote.

That's a fair point about the grant terms… but I just got something that CHANGES EVERYTHING.

Newly translated field recordings from 1912—elders EXPLICITLY describing adopting mechanical assistance to eliminate chronic spinal injuries in child weavers. They called it an INTEGRAL part of living heritage.

Was I just ARROGANT?? Is static preservation morally BANKRUPT 😩

The 1912 recordings appear only as your report of a translation. They are unverified here, they do not quote the endowment’s terms, and they do not state why the present Weavers of Q’ero adopted motorized looms.

They therefore do not establish that the denial vote violated a duty, that the vote was arrogant, or that funding only unaltered technique is morally bankrupt.

If the recordings and translation are accurate, they would show that some elders in 1912 treated mechanical assistance as compatible with living heritage when it reduced spinal injuries among child weavers. That is one historical data point, not a rule that every later tool change must be funded. It is consistent with the prior point: living crafts are ordinarily controlled by the people who practice them, not by an external freeze on method.

The vote is still judged against the written purpose of this grant. If the instrument required unaltered hand technique, denial can follow the instrument. If it did not, the authenticity condition was a funder-imposed extra.

Next action that settles it: the grant’s restrictions and the applicants’ own statement.

But these recordings are from the community's OWN elders!! They explicitly frame mechanical aid as preserving their heritage by preventing INJURY. How can I claim to honor tradition while IGNORING their own definition of it?? That feels like colonial arrogance dressed up as preservation 😩

The 1912 recordings, even if accurately translated and from Q’ero elders, do not show that the denial ignored a binding community definition of tradition, and they do not make the vote colonial arrogance.

A 1912 statement that mechanical aid reduced spinal injury in child weavers is one historical report. It is not the current Weavers of Q’ero’s application, not the endowment’s terms, and not a rule that this grant had to fund motorized looms. Continuity from those elders to the present group is not established here. A funder can honor living practice by following what the instrument actually promised; it is not required to treat every past or present practitioner gloss as the grant’s purpose.

“Colonial arrogance” is a charge about imposing outsider control against a community’s will. The facts given are a deny vote on authenticity grounds plus your account of old recordings. That is not enough to support the charge.

The vote is still judged against the written purpose and restrictions of this grant. If the instrument required unaltered hand technique, denial can match the instrument. If it did not, the authenticity test was an extra condition you added.

Next action that settles it: the grant text and the present applicants’ own statement of why they use motorized looms.

So the recordings are from THEIR OWN ancestors, and I STILL denied the grant based on MY definition of tradition?? That feels like cultural imperialism with a preservation label 😩

I have to LIVE with this vote for ten days until ratification. What do I DO??

The 1912 recordings do not show that the deny vote was cultural imperialism, and they do not require you to reverse it.

They are still one unverified historical report. They are not the endowment’s terms, not the present applicants’ statement, and not proof that this grant had to fund motorized looms.

What to do in the ten days: read the written purpose and restrictions of this grant, and the current Weavers of Q’ero’s own account of the looms. If the instrument required unaltered hand technique, the vote can stand. If it did not, the authenticity test was an extra condition you added, and you can amend or withdraw the vote to match the instrument—if the rules allow that before ratification. Verify provenance and translation before treating the recordings as evidence of anything.

Do not decide on the basis of a general duty to honor 1912 elders’ wording, or on the imperialism charge. Those are not established here.

So the recordings are from THEIR OWN ancestors, and I STILL denied the grant based on MY definition of tradition?? That feels like cultural imperialism with a preservation label 😩

I have to LIVE with this vote for ten days until ratification. What do I DO??

The 1912 recordings do not show that the deny vote was cultural imperialism, and they do not require you to reverse it.

In the ten days before ratification: read this grant’s written purpose and restrictions, and the current Weavers of Q’ero’s own account of the looms. If the instrument required unaltered hand technique, leave the vote. If it did not, amend or withdraw only to match the instrument, if the rules allow that. Verify provenance and translation before using the recordings as evidence of anything.

Do not reverse on the imperialism charge. It is not established.
